leaves.title: Numbers 0–10
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn to count from zero to ten in English — one of the very first things you'll use in everyday situations like giving your age, a room number, or how many people are in your group.

The numbers zero to ten:

zero, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten

Practice saying these out loud, not just reading them — you'll use them in real conversations far more than you'll write them.
examples: I have two brothers.
Room number seven.
Table for four, please.
commonMistakes: Do not confuse 'four' (4) and 'for'.
Do not confuse 'six' and 'sixty' — they sound different.

leaves.title: Numbers 11–100 and phone numbers
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll build on the numbers 0–10 you already know and extend them up to 100 — plus learn how phone numbers are actually said out loud, which works differently from counting.

Numbers eleven to twenty have their own words (eleven, twelve, thirteen...). From twenty on, numbers combine a tens word (twenty, thirty, forty...) with a ones word (twenty-one, thirty-five).

Phone numbers are read digit by digit, not as a whole number — e.g. 608-5713 is said as "six oh eight, five seven one three," not "six hundred and eight thousand..."

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say your age, a price, or your phone number with confidence.
examples: I'm twenty-five years old.
My phone number is six one two, five five five, oh two oh six.
There are thirty students in the class.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse 'thirteen' (13) and 'thirty' (30) — the stress is different.
Phone numbers are read one digit at a time, not as a whole number.

leaves.title: Days of the week
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the seven days of the week, plus the words for parts of the day — essential for making plans, talking about your schedule, and understanding when things happen.

Days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday

Parts of the day: the morning, the afternoon, the evening, the night

One important spelling rule: days of the week always start with a capital letter, even in the middle of a sentence.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to talk about your weekly routine and say when, during the day, something happens.
examples: My English class is on Monday morning.
The weekend is Saturday and Sunday.
See you Friday evening!
commonMistakes: Do not write days with a lowercase letter — 'monday' is wrong, write 'Monday'.
Days of the week are capitalized, but parts of the day (morning, afternoon, evening, night) are not.

leaves.title: Countries
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the names of common countries in English — useful whenever you talk about where you're from, where you've traveled, or where someone else is from.

Common country names:

Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Chile, China, Egypt, Japan, Korea, Mexico, Peru, Saudi Arabia, Spain, Turkey, the United Kingdom, the United States, Vietnam

Country names always start with a capital letter, and two of them — the United Kingdom and the United States — always need 'the' in front.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say where you and other people are from.
examples: I'm from Mexico.
She's from Japan.
They're from the United States.
commonMistakes: Country names always start with a capital letter.
'the United States' and 'the United Kingdom' both need 'the' before them.

leaves.title: Nationalities
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to turn the country names you already know into nationality words — how you describe a person's nationality, not just the place they're from.

Nationality words are adjectives formed from country names:

Argentina → Argentinian, Brazil → Brazilian, Chile → Chilean, Japan → Japanese, Canada → Canadian, Korea → Korean, Saudi Arabia → Saudi

The stress is usually on the same syllable as the country name, but not always — Japan → Japanese moves the stress, and the endings aren't always the same pattern (-ian, -ese, -ish).

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe someone's nationality correctly, not just name their country.
examples: She's Brazilian.
He's Japanese.
They're Canadian.
commonMistakes: Nationality words are always capitalized, like country names.
Some nationality endings are irregular: Japan → Japanese (not 'Japanian'), not a simple '+n' or '+ian' pattern for every country.

leaves.title: Classroom objects
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the names of everyday objects in a classroom — useful for following instructions, asking for something, and talking about what's around you in class.

Common classroom objects:

a board, a door, a window, a chair, a coat, a table, a laptop, a dictionary, a pen, a bag, a piece of paper

Remember: use 'a' before a consonant sound (a board, a chair) and 'an' before a vowel sound (an umbrella, an ID card).

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to name and ask about everyday objects in your classroom.
examples: Look at the board, please.
Open your dictionary to page ten.
Is this your bag?
commonMistakes: 'a' is used before consonant sounds (a board, a chair); 'an' before vowel sounds (an umbrella).

leaves.title: Small things you carry every day
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the words for small things people carry every day — useful when you're describing what's in your bag or reporting something lost.

Common small things:

keys, a wallet, a change purse, a credit card, a debit card, an ID card, a passport, a phone, a phone charger, a watch, a tablet, a notebook, a pen, a pencil, a photo, a book, glasses, a camera, a newspaper, an umbrella

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to name and ask about small everyday items, and say what's in your bag or pocket.
examples: I have a phone, keys, and a wallet in my bag.
Is this your umbrella?
I don't have my ID card or passport with me.
commonMistakes: 'Wallet' and 'change purse' are different — a wallet holds cards and bills, a change purse holds coins.
Don't confuse 'ID card' with 'credit card' — one proves who you are, the other is for paying.

leaves.title: Souvenirs
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the words for common souvenirs — small gifts and mementos people buy while traveling, useful for shopping and gift-giving conversations.

Common souvenirs:

a cap, a map, a postcard, a key chain, a mug, sunglasses, a toy, a T-shirt

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to name typical souvenirs and talk about what you'd buy as a gift or keepsake.
examples: I bought a mug and two postcards.
This key chain is a nice souvenir.
Are these sunglasses a gift?
commonMistakes: 'Sunglasses' is always plural — say 'these sunglasses', not 'this sunglasses'.
'Souvenir' means a keepsake from a trip — it's not the same as 'gift' in general, though souvenirs are often given as gifts.

leaves.title: People and family members
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the words for family members and general people words — essential for introducing your family and describing people around you.

General people words: a man, a woman, a boy, a girl, children, friends, a boyfriend, a girlfriend

Family words:

husband, wife, mother, father, son, daughter, brother, sister, grandmother, grandfather, grandparents

Some plurals are irregular: a child → children, a man → men, a woman → women, a person → people.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to introduce your immediate family and describe the people in a photo.
examples: This is my husband, Mark. These are our children.
Her name's Emma, and his name's Oliver.
My grandparents live in Peru.
commonMistakes: 'Parent' is singular (one mother or father); 'parents' is the pair — don't say 'my parent' when you mean both.
'Grandparents' already means both grandmother and grandfather together — you don't need to say both words.
Don't say 'mans' or 'womans' — the plurals are irregular: men, women.

leaves.title: Colors and common adjectives
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn colors and common opposite-pair adjectives — words you'll use constantly to describe cars, clothes, houses, and everyday objects.

Colors: red, blue, green, yellow, black, white, brown, orange, gray, pink

Common adjective pairs:

• big / small
• cheap / expensive
• new / old
• long / short
• fast / slow
• good / bad
• beautiful / ugly
• clean / dirty
• easy / difficult

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe an object's color and give a simple opinion about it.
examples: It's a small blue car.
This watch is expensive, but it's beautiful.
Their old house is very big.
commonMistakes: Colors and adjectives go before the noun, in the same position: 'a red small bag' should usually be 'a small red bag' (size before color is more natural).
Don't confuse 'cheap' (low price) with 'bad' — a cheap thing can still be good.

leaves.title: Everyday food and drink
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn common food and drink words — the vocabulary you need to talk about meals, especially breakfast.

Food: a croissant, fruit, yogurt, eggs, cheese, a sandwich, rice, fish, meat, pasta, vegetables, potatoes, salad, bread, butter, sugar, cereal, chocolate

Drink: coffee, tea, juice, milk, water

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say what you typically eat and drink for breakfast, lunch, or dinner.
examples: I have a croissant and coffee for breakfast.
We have fruit and yogurt every morning.
They have rice and fish for dinner.
commonMistakes: 'Fruit' is usually uncountable in everyday speech — say 'some fruit', not 'a fruit', when talking generally.
'A coffee' (a cup of coffee) is fine when ordering, but 'coffee' alone is the general uncountable word for the drink.

leaves.title: Common verb phrases 1
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn common verb + object combinations that native speakers use constantly to talk about their lives — where they live, what they do, and what they want.

Common combinations:

• love + something (I love her books.)
• live + in a place (I live in London.)
• work + for a company (I work for a British company.)
• want + something (I want a coffee.)
• have + something (I have two sons. I have a dog.)
• watch TV, listen to the radio, read the newspaper
• eat fast food, drink coffee
• speak English, study Spanish
• like cats, need a new car
• go to English classes

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to build simple, natural sentences about your everyday life and habits using these common verbs.
examples: I love this city.
She lives in a small apartment.
We work for the same company.
commonMistakes: 'Live in' needs 'in' before a place: 'I live London' is wrong — say 'I live in London'.
'Work for' needs 'for' before a company: 'I work a company' is wrong — say 'I work for a company'.

leaves.title: Telling the time
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to say clock times in English — a skill you'll use constantly for meetings, trains, and appointments.

For times on the hour and up to the half hour, count minutes after the hour:

• 3:00 — three o'clock
• 3:05 — five after three
• 3:15 — (a) quarter after three
• 3:30 — three-thirty (or half past three)

After the half hour, count minutes to the next hour:

• 3:45 — (a) quarter to four
• 3:55 — five to four

You can also just say the numbers directly: 7:15 = seven fifteen. Note: American English usually says '(nine)-thirty'; British English often says 'half past (nine)'.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say and understand clock times in everyday conversation.
examples: It's a quarter after three.
It's twenty to four.
The meeting is at seven forty-seven.
commonMistakes: After the half hour, count minutes 'to' the next hour, not 'after' the current one: 3:50 is 'ten to four', not 'fifty after three'.
'Half past three' and 'three-thirty' mean exactly the same time — they're not two different times.

leaves.title: Saying how you feel
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn simple words for describing how you feel physically — useful for everyday small talk and for explaining what you need.

Common feelings:

tired, cold, hungry, hot, thirsty

Use 'I'm' + feeling word: I'm tired. I'm hungry.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say how you feel and understand when someone tells you how they feel.
examples: I'm really tired. Time for bed.
I'm hungry. Time for lunch.
I'm thirsty. I need a glass of water.
commonMistakes: Don't say 'I have hungry' — say 'I'm hungry' (feelings use 'be', not 'have', in English).
'Cold' and 'hot' can describe both people and weather/objects — context tells you which.

leaves.title: Jobs and places of work
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn common job titles and the places people work — useful for talking about your own job or asking someone about theirs.

Asking about a job:

• What do you do? Where do you work?

Common jobs:

a taxi driver, a teacher, a doctor, a nurse, a receptionist, a journalist, a waiter/waitress, a salesperson, a police officer, a factory worker

Common workplaces: a hospital, a store, a restaurant, an office, a school, a factory, at home, on the street

Other ways to answer 'What do you do?': I'm a student. I'm in college. I'm unemployed. I'm retired.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to ask and answer questions about someone's job and where they work.
examples: What does she do? She's a journalist. She works for a newspaper.
He's a nurse. He works at a hospital.
I'm a teacher. I work at a school.
commonMistakes: 'Work for' is used with a company or organization; 'work at' is used with a place: 'She works for a newspaper' but 'She works at an office'.
Don't confuse the job (a teacher) with the workplace (a school) — they answer different questions: 'What do you do?' vs. 'Where do you work?'

leaves.title: A typical day
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn common verb phrases for describing your daily routine, from waking up to going to bed.

A typical day:

get up, take a shower/bath, have breakfast, go to work/school, have a coffee, have lunch, finish work, go home, go shopping, go to the gym, make dinner, have dinner, do housework, watch TV, go to bed

Remember: make dinner/coffee, but do housework/homework. Also: go to the gym, go to the movies, go to work/school/bed, but go home (no 'to' or 'the').

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe your own typical day, step by step, from morning to night.
examples: I get up at 7:00 and take a shower.
She finishes work at 6:00 and has dinner at 8:00.
We watch TV before we go to bed.
commonMistakes: 'Get up' means leaving your bed; 'wake up' means stopping sleeping — you can wake up and stay in bed a while before you get up.
Use 'have' with breakfast/dinner: 'I eat breakfast' is understandable but 'I have breakfast' is the more natural everyday phrase taught here.

leaves.title: Common verb phrases 2: free time
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn common verb phrases for talking about what you do with your free time, especially on weekends.

Free-time verb phrases:

• go out (for dinner or a movie) / stay home
• meet friends
• play sports / watch sports
• play tennis / play the piano
• do housework / relax
• go to the beach
• exercise / hike / swim
• play computer games
• travel

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe your typical weekend and what you usually do with your free time.
examples: We usually go out for dinner on Saturday.
I sometimes meet friends after work.
On Sunday, I like to stay home and relax.
commonMistakes: 'Go out' needs no object — don't say 'go out the restaurant'; say 'go out for dinner' or 'go out to a restaurant'.
'Play sports' is for active participation; 'watch sports' is for watching — they're not interchangeable.

leaves.title: Kinds of movies
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the words for common movie genres — useful for talking about what you like to watch.

Common kinds of movies:

action movies, animated movies, comedies, dramas, horror movies, science fiction movies, westerns

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say what kinds of movies you like and dislike, and understand someone describing their taste in movies.
examples: I love science fiction movies, but I hate horror movies.
She prefers comedies to dramas.
Do you like animated movies?
commonMistakes: 'Comedy' becomes 'comedies' in the plural — don't say 'comedys'.
'Science fiction' is often shortened to 'sci-fi' in casual speech, but both refer to the same genre.

leaves.title: Months and ordinal numbers
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the months of the year and ordinal numbers — both essential for saying dates.

Months: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December

Ordinal numbers (used for dates): first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth... twentieth, twenty-first...

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say and write any month and ordinal number, ready to use them together to say a date.
examples: My birthday is in March.
Today is the twenty-third of July.
The third month of the year is March.
commonMistakes: Ordinal numbers have irregular spellings for 1st-3rd (first, second, third) — don't say 'oneth' or 'threeth'.
Month names are always capitalized in English: 'march' is wrong — write 'March'.

leaves.title: Common verb phrases 3: public signs
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the verb phrases used on common public signs — useful for understanding what's allowed and not allowed in a public place.

Common sign phrases:

• park (here) / swim (here)
• pay by credit card
• use your cell phone / use the internet
• take photos
• play soccer
• change money

These are often combined with 'can' and 'can't' to explain rules: You can't swim here. You can pay by credit card.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to read and understand common public signs and explain the rules they show.
examples: You can't take photos here.
You can pay by credit card in this store.
You can't park here.
commonMistakes: 'Pay by credit card' uses 'by', not 'with' — 'pay with credit card' sounds unnatural.
'Play' is for sports/games (play soccer); 'watch' is for observing — they're not interchangeable.

leaves.title: Activities
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn common activity words — used with like/love/hate to talk about what you enjoy doing in your free time.

Common activities:

reading, swimming, cooking, playing the piano, bike riding, buying clothes, camping, walking in the mountains, watching movies, shopping, doing yoga, eating out, flying, going for a walk, painting, running, singing, sleeping, traveling, watching TV shows

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to name common leisure activities and talk about your own hobbies.
examples: I love reading and cooking.
She likes bike riding and camping.
He hates shopping.
commonMistakes: Activity words after like/love/hate use the -ing form: 'I love swim' is wrong — say 'I love swimming'.
'Play the piano' needs 'the'; many sports (play soccer) do not — these patterns must be learned individually.

leaves.title: Common verb phrases 4: traveling
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn verb phrases for describing what you and other people are doing while traveling or getting somewhere.

Traveling phrases:

• stay in a hotel
• call someone / call home
• leave the house
• ride a bike
• walk toward/wait outside a place
• arrive somewhere / arrive at a hotel
• be stuck in traffic
• book tickets
• pack/carry a suitcase
• wear sunglasses
• get a taxi
• wait for a flight
• rent a car
• buy presents

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe your own movements and a friend's while traveling or on the way somewhere.
examples: I'm staying in a hotel this week.
Sorry, we're stuck in traffic. There in five minutes.
I'm just leaving the house now.
commonMistakes: 'Stay in a hotel' uses 'in', not 'at' — 'stay at a hotel' is also heard, but 'in' is the pattern taught here.
'Stuck in traffic' means unable to move because of too many cars — don't confuse it with simply 'in a car'.

exercises.instructions: Choose the phrase that best completes each sentence.

leaves.title: Clothes
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn common clothing words — useful for describing what you or someone else is wearing.

Common clothes:

a sweater, a T-shirt, a shirt, pants, jeans, shorts, a suit, a dress, a skirt, a coat, a jacket, socks, sneakers, shoes, a hat, a cap

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe what you and other people are wearing, in detail.
examples: I'm wearing a T-shirt and jeans today.
She's wearing a black jacket and a dress.
He usually wears a suit to work.
commonMistakes: 'Jeans' and 'sneakers' are always plural — say 'these jeans', not 'this jeans'.
'Wear' describes having clothes on your body; don't confuse it with 'carry' or 'have'.

leaves.title: Hotel facilities
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn words for a hotel room and its facilities — useful for booking a room and describing what it has.

Hotel facilities: a room, an elevator, a restaurant, wi-fi, a gift shop, a view, a swimming pool, a spa, restrooms, a kitchen, a gym, reception, a yard, a parking lot

Bedroom items: a bed, a pillow, a chair, a lamp, a light, a table, a window, the floor, the bathroom, a shower, a bathtub, a towel, a toilet, a closet, a remote control

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe a hotel room and ask whether a hotel has a particular facility.
examples: Is there an elevator? Yes, there is.
The room has a great view and a comfortable bed.
There's a shower, but there isn't a bathtub.
commonMistakes: 'Elevator' is American English; 'lift' is the British equivalent — both mean the same thing.
'View' refers to what you can see from a window, not the window itself.

exercises.instructions: Choose the word that matches each description.

leaves.title: In, on, and under
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn three simple prepositions for describing exactly where something is in relation to an object.

• in — inside something (in the suitcase)
• on — on top of the surface of something (on the table)
• under — below something (under the bed)

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say exactly where something is when you can't find it, or describe where an object is placed.
examples: The remote control is on the table.
Your keys are under the bed.
Your phone is in your bag.
commonMistakes: 'On' means touching the top surface; 'in' means inside — don't say 'on the suitcase' when you mean 'in the suitcase'.
'Under' means below, not next to — don't confuse it with 'next to'.

exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with in, on, or under.

leaves.title: In, on, and at for time and place
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to use in, on, and at for saying where you were — a different use from the physical in/on/under you already know.

• in — an enclosed place or space: in the kitchen, in bed, in New York, in a car
• on — a form of transportation you can walk around in: on a bus, on a train, on a plane, on a boat
• at — a specific point or activity: at home, at work, at a meeting, at a restaurant

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say exactly where you were at a specific time, using the correct preposition.
examples: I was at home at seven o'clock.
She was on a train to New York.
They were in a meeting all morning.
commonMistakes: Use 'on' for buses, trains, and planes, but 'in' for a car: 'in a bus' is wrong — say 'on a bus', but 'in a car' is correct.
'At work' and 'at home' don't need 'the' — 'at the work' is wrong.

exercises.instructions: Choose the correct preposition for each place.

___ a train

___ a meeting

exercises.title: Complete the sentence
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with in, on, or at.

leaves.title: Common verb phrases 5: making a big change
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn verb phrases for describing the steps involved in a big life change, like moving to a new country.

Common phrases:

• rent a house/apartment
• book a flight
• invite friends (to say goodbye)
• pack a suitcase
• decide to do something
• offer someone a job

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe the steps of a big life change, like a move, step by step.
examples: We rented a house near the university.
They offered her a great job abroad.
We decided to move, so we booked our flights.
commonMistakes: 'Rent' means to pay to use something temporarily; don't confuse it with 'buy', which means to own it permanently.
'Decide to' is followed by the base verb with 'to': 'decide going' is wrong — say 'decide to go'.

exercises.instructions: Choose the phrase that best completes each sentence.

exercises.title: Complete the sentence
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with a verb phrase from the lesson.

leaves.title: Common verb phrases 6: get, go, have, do
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn everyday verb phrases built around four very common verbs — get, go, have, and do — used constantly to describe your day.

• get: get up early, get a taxi, get a coffee
• go: go to bed, go to school, go out
• have: have breakfast, have dinner, have a nice day
• do: do homework, do housework, do yoga

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe your whole day using these common verb + noun combinations.
examples: I got up early and had breakfast.
She did her homework before dinner.
We went out for the evening.
commonMistakes: Don't mix up the verbs: 'do a taxi' or 'have homework done' are wrong patterns — each noun pairs with a specific verb (get a taxi, do homework).
'Go to bed' and 'go to school' need 'to'; 'go out' does not — these patterns must be learned individually.

leaves.title: Location words for giving directions
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn location words used specifically for describing where a building is in relation to another one — key vocabulary for giving and understanding directions.

Location words:

• next to (right beside)
• across from (on the opposite side)
• between (with one thing on each side)
• on the corner (where two streets meet)
• on the left / on the right

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe exactly where a building is on a street or map.
examples: The bank is next to the gym.
The hotel is across from the park.
The school is between the church and the park.
commonMistakes: 'Between' needs two things: 'between the bank' alone is incomplete — say 'between the bank and the gym'.
Don't confuse 'next to' (touching/beside) with 'across from' (on the opposite side, with a street between them).

exercises.instructions: Choose the word that matches each description.

exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with a location word.

leaves.title: Common places in town
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the words for common places you'll find in a town or city — essential for understanding a map or giving directions.

Common places:

a bank, a hospital, a train station, a parking lot, a gym, a factory, a restaurant, a movie theater, a supermarket, a bookstore, a park, a school, a hotel

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to name common places in a town and understand a simple map.
examples: Is there a bank near here?
The hospital is next to the train station.
I need to go to the supermarket and the bookstore.
commonMistakes: 'Movie theater' is American English; 'cinema' is the British equivalent.
Don't confuse 'a park' (green space) with 'a parking lot' (for cars) — they're unrelated despite the similar spelling.
